title: Test-time Domain Generalization for Image Super-resolution
one_liner: Adjust a low-quality image at test time by matching each small image part to source-domain parts that the model already knows how to restore.
lead: A super-resolution model learns from one kind of image and then meets a different kind at test time. Usual test-time fixes change broad style cues, but super-resolution depends on fine local detail. This paper instead matches small image parts to learned source-domain parts so the adjustment happens at the level where restoration errors actually begin.

problem.h2: Why broad style transfer is too coarse
paras: Test-time domain generalization tries to help a trained model handle new data without retraining. Many methods do this by pushing the new sample toward the look of the training data. That can help for image-level tasks because broad appearance cues may be enough there, but super-resolution predicts pixels, so broad style fixes miss the small local patterns that decide whether edges and textures are restored correctly.

If a low-quality target image has local structures that differ from the source images, the model can fail even when the overall style looks close. The problem is local because each pixel prediction depends on nearby image evidence.

callout.html: Learn source-domain part libraries and use test-time matching to rewrite target features at the pixel level so the super-resolution model sees patterns it already knows how to repair.

paras: The paper changes the adaptation unit. Instead of changing the whole image feature style at once, it adapts each local position using learned part libraries, because super-resolution errors are created and fixed at that smaller scale.

hidden.name: local source match quality
paras: The hidden quantity is how well each target location matches a source-domain part that the model already understands. When the match is good, the model sees a familiar local pattern and can restore it more reliably because training taught it how that pattern should expand into a high-resolution patch.

MC-TTDG raises this quantity by storing both shared parts and source-specific parts. The shared parts cover common structure, and the source-specific parts cover fine appearance details that broad adaptation methods blur away.

heat.caption: Darker cells mark target locations with stronger matches to known source-domain parts.

reads.html: The method works when each small image region can be aligned with a source-domain region that the model already knows how to sharpen.
Pixel-level nearest-neighbor transfer uses shared and source-specific part libraries so target features move toward source features that support accurate reconstruction.

paras: A super-resolution network maps local low-quality evidence to local high-quality detail. When a target image comes from a new domain, that local evidence can fall outside what the network saw in training, so the output becomes blurry or wrong.

MC-TTDG fixes this by rewriting target features at each location. The nearest source-domain part gives a concrete reference for what that local pattern should look like in the model's internal space, so the following restoration layers operate on inputs that are closer to training-time conditions.

The domain-choice vote matters because the best source-specific library can differ from one target image to another. Picking the library by consensus reduces poor matches because several local signals must agree before one source domain is chosen.

math.words: For each target location, choose the source-domain part with the smallest feature distance and use it to adjust the target feature before reconstruction.

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: A target edge patch has feature value 7.2.
Candidate source-domain parts have values 6.9, 7.1, and 8.4.
The closest value is 7.1, so that source part is selected.
The target feature is adjusted toward 7.1 before reconstruction.
That helps because the model learned during training how to sharpen patterns near 7.1.

math.note: The full method uses many positions and many stored parts, but the main rule stays the same: move each target location toward a familiar source-domain part.

items.html: If the target image contains local patterns absent from every source domain, nearest-part transfer can still miss because the chosen part is only the least bad option.

items.b: Wrong source library wins the vote.
items.html: If the target image mixes several domain traits, the vote may favor one source library that only fits part of the image, so some locations are adjusted in the wrong direction.

items.b: Part transfer may oversmooth rare details.
items.html: A rare fine structure can be replaced by a more common source-domain pattern when the nearest stored part is too generic.
The method works best when the source domains span many local textures because wider coverage raises the chance that each target location finds a useful match.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Train a super-resolution model on one or more source domains, then test it on a different target domain without fine-tuning. Compare three cases: no test-time adaptation, broad style adjustment, and MC-TTDG local part transfer.
Measure reconstruction quality and inspect edge regions. MC-TTDG should restore sharper local structure because it aligns each target location with known source-domain detail.
demo.closing: The demo should make clear that pixel-level transfer matters more than broad style transfer when the task lives or dies by fine local detail.
